prompt: Where does the code of a Playwright test run?

choices.text: In a Node process outside the browser
choices.why: Right. The test stays in Node and reaches the browser over one connection.

choices.text: Inside the page, beside the shop's own scripts
choices.why: That is Cypress's arrangement, from lesson 9; Playwright keeps the test out of the page.

choices.text: In a driver program such as chromedriver
choices.why: A driver program is Selenium's middle step, from lesson 8; Playwright has none.

choices.text: On a Playwright server on the internet
choices.why: Nothing leaves your machine: the test, the browser and the shop all run on it.

prompt: `look.mjs` printed every response the moment it arrived, without asking the browser in a loop. What in Playwright's design makes that possible?

choices.text: The browser sends events up the connection unasked
choices.why: Right. Commands go down and events come up on the same open connection.

choices.text: Playwright polls the page every few milliseconds
choices.why: Polling is what a one-way protocol forces on a tool; the connection here is two-way.

choices.text: The test runs inside the page and sees each request
choices.why: The test runs in Node, outside the page.

choices.text: The shop logs each request to Playwright
choices.why: The shop's log goes to its own terminal; it knows nothing about Playwright.

prompt: Match each tool, or browser, to how a test reaches it.

pairs.right: One HTTP request per command, to a driver
The test is loaded into the browser itself
A patched build with its own protocol

prompt: `tests/contexts.spec.js` holds four tests. How many test runs does `npx playwright test --config browsers.config.js tests/contexts.spec.js` start, with all three browsers installed?
`npx playwright test --config browsers.config.js --project chromium tests/smoke.spec.js` answers `Project(s) "tests/smoke.spec.js" not found`. What is wrong?

choices.text: The file is missing from `tests/`
choices.why: The message is about a project name, and the name it quotes is the file.

choices.text: `--project` swallowed the file name as a second project
choices.why: Right. Write `--project=chromium`, or put the files before the option.

choices.text: `browsers.config.js` has no project called chromium
choices.why: The same message lists the available projects, and chromium is the first.

choices.text: A separate config cannot be combined with --project
choices.why: It can; the run with `--project=chromium` worked with the same config.

prompt: A team's users all browse with Google Chrome, and a defect appears only there. Which project setting puts that browser under the tests?

choices.text: `devices['Desktop Chrome']`
choices.why: That describes a window and a user agent and still runs Playwright's own Chromium.

choices.text: `channel: 'chrome'`
choices.why: Right. A channel runs the branded browser installed on the computer.

choices.text: `npx playwright install firefox`
choices.why: That downloads Playwright's patched Firefox, which is not Chrome at all.

choices.text: Nothing: Chromium and Chrome are one program
choices.why: They share an engine and differ in what Google adds, which is where such a defect can live.

choices.text: A fresh profile inside one browser
choices.why: Right. Its own cookies, storage and cache, like a private window.

choices.text: A second browser process started for each test
choices.why: The browser is started once per worker; contexts are made inside it in milliseconds.

choices.text: Another name for a tab
choices.why: A tab is a page, and a context can hold several pages.

choices.text: The settings in `playwright.config.js`
choices.why: The configuration supplies options to contexts; it is not one.

prompt: Ana and Bia each have a context of their own. Bia opens the shop having added nothing, and her basket says 1. Why?

choices.text: Bia's context shares Ana's localStorage
choices.why: The first test showed the opposite: Bia's page read `null`.

choices.text: The shop keeps one basket on the server for everybody
choices.why: Right. A context isolates what the browser keeps, and the basket is not in the browser.

choices.text: A cookie from Ana's context leaked to Bia
choices.why: Both printed `[]`: the shop sets no cookie at all.

choices.text: The reset in `beforeEach` did not run
choices.why: It ran; the banana was added after it, by Ana, in the same test.

prompt: A test writes a value into `localStorage` through the `page` fixture. The next test in the file reads it. What does it get?

choices.text: The value, because the browser is the same
choices.why: The browser is the same; the context is not, and storage belongs to the context.

choices.text: `null`, because each test gets its own context
choices.why: Right. That is Playwright's default, and the last test of the file shows it.

choices.text: An error, because storage is cleared by force
choices.why: Nothing is cleared; the new context simply never had the value.

choices.text: The value, unless the tests run in two workers
choices.why: Even in one worker each test has a new context.

prompt: Which of these does a new browser context start without? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The cookies another context received
choices.why: Right. Cookies belong to the context that received them.

choices.text: Values written to `localStorage` in another context
choices.why: Right. Bia's page read `null` where Ana's read `ana`.

choices.text: Lines added to the shop's basket by another context
choices.why: The basket is on the server, and every context sees the same one.

choices.text: Files cached by another context
choices.why: Right. The cache is part of the profile a context isolates.

prompt: Order these from the one that holds the others to the one held.
trap: A context is inside a browser, not the other way round: one browser holds many contexts.

prompt: Straight after clicking Add to basket, `await count.textContent()` returned `0`, and `await expect(count).toHaveText('1')` then passed. Why did they disagree?

choices.text: The click failed the first time and was retried
choices.why: One click, one request; only the reading differed.

choices.text: `textContent()` reads the page once; the assertion reads until it matches
choices.why: Right. The snapshot came before the shop's answer; the assertion waited for it.

choices.text: The count is drawn inside a frame that a plain read of the page cannot reach
choices.why: There is no frame; the read reached the element and got its text at that instant.

choices.text: `toHaveText` ignores digits
choices.why: It compared `1` with `1`; the earlier failing run shows it comparing digits exactly.

prompt: With the configuration this course uses, an assertion on a locator gives up after ___ seconds, and a whole test after ___ seconds.
A click fails with `Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded` and a call log that only ever says `waiting for getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' })`. What is the first thing to suspect?

choices.text: The locator matches nothing on the page
choices.why: Right. It never resolved; a button that existed but was covered or disabled would have been found first.

choices.text: The action timeout of five seconds is too short
choices.why: Five seconds is the assertion's clock; the click waited thirty, the whole test.

choices.text: The button was found but held the wrong text
choices.why: A found element shows as `locator resolved to` in the call log.

choices.text: The browser crashed during the test
choices.why: A crashed browser fails with a different message, not a call log still waiting.

prompt: After `npx playwright test --trace on`, where is each test's trace?

choices.text: Printed in the terminal, in the summary at the end of the run
choices.why: The run's output does not mention the trace at all.

choices.text: In `playwright-report/`, inside the HTML report
choices.why: That folder is written by the HTML reporter; traces go elsewhere.

choices.text: A `trace.zip` in a folder per test, in `test-results/`
choices.why: Right. Each folder is named after the file and the test.

choices.text: On Playwright's website
choices.why: Nothing is uploaded; the trace is a file on your disk.

prompt: Put the steps of reading a failing test's trace in order.
trap: There is nothing to open before a run has recorded it.

prompt: Recording a trace of every test costs disk and time. What does Playwright's documentation suggest for a suite that runs on a build server?

choices.text: Never record traces on a server
choices.why: The server is where nobody watches, so it is where a trace earns its place.

choices.text: `trace: 'on-first-retry'`, recording when a failed test is retried
choices.why: Right. Passing tests cost nothing, and a failure leaves its evidence.

choices.text: Screenshots only
choices.why: A trace holds screenshots and also the actions, requests and console, which is why it is worth more.

choices.text: `--trace on` for every run
choices.why: That is the costly setting the question starts from.

prompt: Two tests in different files each add a banana and expect the count to read 1. Alone, each passes. With two workers, one fails reading 2. Which change would make both pass?

choices.text: Give each test its own browser context
choices.why: They already have one each; the basket is on the server, out of a context's reach.

choices.text: Run them one at a time, with one worker
choices.why: Right, for now: the shared basket is the cause, and lessons 15 and 19 deal with it properly.

choices.text: Raise the assertion timeout to thirty seconds
choices.why: Waiting longer does not turn a 2 into a 1.

choices.text: Run them in Firefox as well
choices.why: A second engine runs the same tests against the same basket.

prompt: A test passes in the chromium project and fails in webkit on a teammate's machine. Your machine has only Chromium. What is the most useful next step?

choices.text: Delete the webkit project, since Chromium passes
choices.why: That hides the one finding the project exists to make.

choices.text: Ask for the trace of the failing webkit run
choices.why: Right. The trace holds the actions, the page and the network of that run, and opening it needs no WebKit.

choices.text: Run the chromium project again until it fails
choices.why: The failure is in another engine; repeating this one measures nothing new.

choices.text: Change `devices['Desktop Safari']` to `devices['Desktop Chrome']`
choices.why: That turns the webkit project into a second Chromium run.
